questions.question: You receive an email saying your Microsoft account will be deactivated in 10 minutes unless you click a link to verify your identity. What should you do?

choices.label: Click the link quickly — you can't afford to lose access to your account
choices.hint: Acting fast is exactly what the attacker wants.

choices.label: Slow down, ignore the link, and go directly to the official Microsoft site by typing the address yourself
choices.hint: Navigating directly bypasses any fake links entirely.

choices.label: Reply to the email asking for more time
choices.hint: Replying confirms your email is active and may invite more attacks.

choices.label: Forward it to a colleague to see if they got the same one
choices.hint: This spreads the phishing email to others without resolving anything.

questions.explanation: Urgency is a manipulation tactic. Real account issues don't require you to act in minutes. Always navigate directly to the official site rather than clicking links in unexpected emails.

questions.question: You receive an email that appears to be from your CFO asking you to urgently purchase five $200 gift cards for a client and send them the codes. The email says to keep it quiet and not go through normal channels. What do you do?

choices.label: Purchase the gift cards — it would be embarrassing to question the CFO
choices.hint: Authority pressure is a common social engineering tactic.

choices.label: Reply to the email asking for a purchase order number
choices.hint: The attacker controls this inbox and will provide a convincing answer.

choices.label: Contact the CFO directly through a phone number or method you already know — not anything from the email
choices.hint: Verifying through a separate, trusted channel is the right move.

choices.label: Purchase the cards and report it to finance afterward
choices.hint: Once the codes are shared, the money is gone and unrecoverable.

questions.explanation: This is a classic Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack. Your organization will never ask you to purchase gift cards via email. When a request comes with pressure to skip normal steps, always verify through a separate channel you already trust.

questions.question: An email claiming to be from your company's legal team states: "Your account has been used for suspicious activity. Failure to respond within 2 hours will result in legal escalation." What is the safest response?

choices.label: Follow the instructions in the email immediately to avoid consequences
choices.hint: Fear is the tactic — acting on it is the trap.

choices.label: Contact HR or your IT team directly using contact details you already know
choices.hint: Independent verification is always the right step.

choices.label: Reply to the email to find out what suspicious activity occurred
choices.hint: Replying engages the attacker and may give them useful information.

choices.label: Change your password immediately using the link in the email
choices.hint: This link likely leads to a fake page designed to steal your new password.

questions.explanation: Real legal or HR notices always include proper context, reference numbers, and official channels. They never demand action through an email link within hours. Verify independently before doing anything.

questions.question: A colleague receives an email saying: "Hi Sarah, I've attached the updated budget from our Monday call — let me know if the figures look right." The email looks convincing but the sender domain is slightly different from your company's. What type of attack is this most likely?

choices.label: Generic phishing — sent to thousands of people at once
choices.hint: Generic phishing uses mass targeting, not personal details.

choices.label: Spear phishing — targeted and personalized to appear credible
choices.hint: Personal context and a specific target are the hallmarks of spear phishing.

choices.label: Smishing — delivered via text message
choices.hint: Smishing is SMS-based, not email.

choices.label: Quishing — delivered via a QR code
choices.hint: Quishing involves QR codes embedded in messages or physical materials.

questions.explanation: Spear phishing uses personal or workplace context — names, meeting references, roles — to appear legitimate. The subtle domain difference is the key red flag here. Always check sender addresses carefully on any unexpected email with an attachment.

questions.question: You receive a text message: "Your FedEx delivery failed. Update your delivery preferences here: c7dvr.info/GtK12vilM". You weren't expecting a package. What should you do?

choices.label: Tap the link to check — it might be a legitimate delivery
choices.hint: Short, unfamiliar links in unexpected texts are a major red flag.

choices.label: Reply with your address to reschedule the delivery
choices.hint: Replying provides personal information to the attacker.

choices.label: Ignore it and if genuinely concerned, go directly to the FedEx website yourself
choices.hint: Navigating directly bypasses any fake link entirely.

choices.label: Forward it to the company's security team and then tap the link
choices.hint: Reporting is correct, but you should not tap the link at all.

questions.explanation: This is smishing — phishing via SMS. Unrecognizable short links in unsolicited texts are a clear warning sign. If you're genuinely concerned about a delivery, always go directly to the carrier's official website rather than using any link from the text.

questions.question: Which of the following would your organization's IT team or leadership legitimately ask you to do via email?

choices.label: Provide your current password to verify your account
choices.hint: No legitimate IT team ever needs your password.

choices.label: Scan a QR code in the email to validate your credentials
choices.hint: Credential validation via QR code in email is a red flag.

choices.label: Click a link to reset your password when you have requested a reset yourself
choices.hint: Password reset links you requested yourself are expected and legitimate.

choices.label: Transfer funds to a new vendor account urgently without going through finance
choices.hint: Bypassing normal financial processes is never legitimate.

questions.explanation: A password reset link you specifically requested is legitimate. Your organization will never email you asking for your password, ask you to validate credentials via a QR code, or request financial transfers that bypass your normal approval process.

questions.question: An email arrives saying: "Congratulations! You've been selected for an exclusive employee reward. Only the first 50 respondents get a $150 Amazon gift card — claim yours before midnight." What's the right move?

choices.label: Click the link quickly so you don't miss out
choices.hint: The time pressure and prize are designed to make you act without thinking.

choices.label: Verify the offer through your HR portal or internal communications before doing anything
choices.hint: Checking through official channels confirms whether the offer is real.

choices.label: Forward it to colleagues so they can claim the reward too
choices.hint: Forwarding spreads a phishing email to others.

choices.label: Click the link but don't enter any personal information
choices.hint: Just visiting a malicious page can sometimes be enough to cause harm.

questions.explanation: Scarcity and prize language are designed to trigger FOMO and bypass your judgment. Legitimate employee rewards are always communicated through official HR channels, not unsolicited emails with countdown deadlines. Verify first.

questions.question: Someone calls claiming to be from your company's IT helpdesk. They say a virus has been detected on your computer and they need you to install a remote access tool so they can fix it immediately. What do you do?

choices.label: Follow their instructions — it sounds serious and you don't want a virus
choices.hint: Urgency over the phone is as much a red flag as urgency in email.

choices.label: Ask for their employee ID and then proceed with the installation
choices.hint: An attacker can provide a fake ID number.

choices.label: Hang up and call your IT helpdesk back using a number from your company's official directory
choices.hint: Calling back through a number you already trust confirms whether the call was real.

choices.label: Install the tool but watch closely to make sure they don't access anything sensitive
choices.hint: Once someone has remote access to your computer, they control what you see.

questions.explanation: This is vishing — voice phishing. Your real IT team will never cold call you asking to install remote access software. Hang up and call the helpdesk back using a number from your company directory or intranet. Never install software at the request of an unsolicited caller.

questions.question: Which of the following is the strongest signal that an email is likely a phishing attempt?

choices.label: It uses your correct name and job title
choices.hint: Attackers can easily find names and titles from LinkedIn or company websites.

choices.label: It tells you not to contact IT or your manager and to act immediately via the link provided
choices.hint: Discouraging verification is a hallmark of phishing.

choices.label: It is well-written with no spelling mistakes
choices.hint: Modern phishing emails are often grammatically polished.

choices.label: It comes from an address you don't recognize but the email looks professional
choices.hint: Professionalism alone is not a safety indicator.

questions.explanation: The clearest sign of a phishing attempt is when an email actively discourages you from verifying it. Any legitimate communication from IT, HR, or a vendor will support — not block — your ability to confirm its authenticity.

questions.question: A vendor sends an email saying: "We've updated our banking details. Please use the new account information attached for all future payments. This is urgent as our previous account is being closed." What should you do?

choices.label: Update the payment details — the vendor needs to be paid on time
choices.hint: This is one of the most common and costly types of fraud in corporate environments.

choices.label: Call the vendor back on a phone number from your records — not from the email — to confirm the change
choices.hint: Independent verification through a known channel is the correct step.

choices.label: Reply to the email asking them to confirm the new details
choices.hint: If the email account is compromised, the attacker will confirm the fake details.

choices.label: Forward to finance and ask them to handle it
choices.hint: Finance also needs to be aware this could be fraud — flag it clearly, don't just forward.

questions.explanation: This is invoice fraud / Business Email Compromise. Attackers intercept or spoof vendor emails and redirect payments to fraudulent accounts. Any change to payment details must be verified by calling the vendor directly using a phone number from your existing records — never from the email itself.
